chapter_theme: Sangili Siddhar's kummi, sung to the 'blissful girl' (ஆனந்தப் பெண்ணே), opens with a lineage (Thirumular as guru, the siddha host) and a climb through the body's centres by their presiding gods, Ganesha at the root, the Brahmin in the navel lotus, Vishnu and Lakshmi, Rudra and Rudri, Sadasiva's feet, with the breath (வாசி) as the horse that carries the climb. Its second half turns on the body: a filthy carcass, a salted pot, a bellows, a wedding that becomes a corpse-show, and everything born of earth returning to earth, in which the Lord nonetheless clings like oil in sesame.
structure_note: Twenty-five kummi stanzas with one refrain. 2109 to 2112 are invocation and the letters of Om; 2113 to 2122 are the yoga of breath and the six centres with their gods, closing on self-knowledge and the mantra of mother and father; 2123 to 2128 are the body as fort, pot, bellows and corpse; 2129 to 2133 are the earth argument: all things come from earth, go back to earth, and nothing (parents, body, kin, wife) is சதம், lasting. The chapter break at 2133 is the editor's; the question of 2133 is answered in 2134.

2109.reading: Praising the feet of the Ganesha at the root, hold in your mind the feet of Valai, Tripurai, the Mother, in the supreme awareness that is the threefold flame everywhere, blissful girl.
2109.nuance: மூலக் கணேசன் is Ganesha as the god of the root centre (மூலாதாரம்) in the traditional scheme of six centres, each with its deity; the stanzas that follow climb that scheme. முச்சுடர் is tradition's sun, moon and fire. வாலை and திரிபுரை are the young goddess and the goddess of the three cities, here one Mother; the refrain's ஆனந்தப் பெண் may be the same goddess, the listener, or the poet's own soul.

2110.reading: Our guru is Thirumular; one who has always praised and hymned his feet should bow to the feet of the host of great siddhas who are free of doubt, blissful girl.
2110.nuance: The claim of Thirumular as guru is a lineage claim and not a date; 2135 and 2144 add Bogar as the poet's பாட்டன் (grandfather, or guru's guru). The siddhas are praised as a community (குழாம்), as the Tirumanthiram praises the devotees.

2111.reading: The circle of Om became the body, and then the mute letter became the life; know yourself the way in which it becomes ரீங்காரம் and ஸ்ரீங்காரம், blissful girl.
2111.nuance: ஊமை எழுத்து, the mute letter, is tradition's name for the unsounded part of Om (the final nasal or the half-measure); the stanza makes Om the body and the silent part of Om the life in it. ரீம் and ஸ்ரீம் are seed syllables of the goddess, as the next stanza's letters are those of the five-letter mantra. The plain claim is that body and life are made of sound; the particulars are the cipher.

2112.reading: When அ joins உ it becomes ய; knowing that, stand in the clarity that is சி and discern, blissful girl.
2112.nuance: The arithmetic of letters is not grammar: tradition reads அ as Siva, உ as Shakti, and ய as the soul, the letter of the five-letter mantra that stands for the bound soul, with சி as Siva's own letter. So read, the stanza says the soul arises from Siva and Shakti and must stand in Siva. The stanza itself gives only the letters.

2113.reading: Will those who have seen and known the five elements think even a little of attachment to this world? Know the way of yoga yourself, without agitation, and be saved, blissful girl.

2114.reading: To those who know the state of tapas it becomes known through jnana itself; so know well what the nine siddhas and the others saw and made clear, blissful girl.
2114.nuance: நவசித்தர், the nine siddhas, is a traditional list (its members vary by source); the stanza invokes them as authorities, so the knowledge is handed down as well as seen.

2115.reading: If you know the state of the breath, the mind, pleased that tapas is accomplished, mounts the horse called தேசி and makes its search; know that, blissful girl.
2115.nuance: The horse is the Siddhars' standing figure for the breath, and tradition hears வாசி itself as the horse; தேசி (shining, or of the country) is the horse's name here. The claim is that knowing the breath is the whole of tapas (தவம் வாய்த்தது), a stronger claim than 2114, where tapas is known through jnana.

2116.reading: Those who have known Nandi's court never give up the quest of the breath; know well the seat of the Brahmin in the navel lotus and be saved, blissful girl.
2116.nuance: அந்தணன், the Brahmin, is read by tradition as Brahma, the god of the second centre in the six-centre scheme, though the stanza places him at the navel (உந்தி), which the scheme gives to Vishnu. நந்தி கொலு, Nandi's court or audience, is the Lord's seat at the crown, or the guru's presence. The ascent continues in 2117 and 2118.

2117.reading: Bowing at the place where Vishnu and Lakshmi dwell and passing beyond it, you will go on and see above the service of Rudra and Rudri, blissful girl.
2117.nuance: The gods are stations of the climb: Vishnu's centre and Rudra's centre, each with his consort, in the traditional assignment of deities to the centres. The stanza says only that one bows and passes on; where in the body these places are is tradition's gloss.

2118.reading: Whatever puja one performs, even if one has seen and known that the Supreme is one, is not the means by which thought subsides the fine feet of Sadasiva, blissful girl?
2118.nuance: The stanza places both ritual and the monist's knowledge (பரம் ஏகம்) below the stilling of thought, and makes the Lord's feet the means of that stilling. Sadasiva is the god of the highest centre in the scheme the stanzas have climbed.

2119.reading: Knowing as 'I myself am I' the arising that is the Siva-Supreme which stands filled as itself alone, know the supreme quest, blissful girl.
2119.nuance: உற்பனம் (also 2141, பர உற்பனம்) is an arising or appearance, here of the Supreme as oneself. நானே நான் is the first-person form of the great saying; what fills everything is known as 'I'. The stanza follows 2118, which made the feet the means, so the identity is reached by the feet and not by assertion.

2120.reading: Knowing that deceitful birth and death are no more than a residual trace that goes before, if you do pranayama without agitation you become the Supreme, blissful girl.
2120.nuance: வாசனை is the trace or latent impression that carries the soul from birth to birth; the stanza makes birth and death themselves that trace, and sets pranayama alone as what dissolves it. The promise, தற்பரம் ஆவாய், is as strong as the Tirumanthiram's சிவன் அவன் ஆமே.

2121.reading: Even having passed beyond chariyai and kiriyai, even having achieved yoga and received grace, without the proper letting-go of jnana nothing is of any use, blissful girl.
2121.nuance: ஞான விசர்க்கம் is obscure: விசர்க்கம் (visarga) is a release or discharge, so perhaps the letting-go that jnana is, or the jnana that lets go; a copyist's slip for விசாரம் (inquiry) is possible. Either way the four Saiva paths are ranked with jnana as the only one that counts.

2122.reading: If one knows oneself as 'this is what I am', must one then still go looking for the Supreme? The one who knows the mantra that mother and father taught is the jnani, blissful girl.
2122.nuance: அன்னையும் அப்பனும் may be the parents, or Shakti and Siva as the teaching pair, which tradition prefers and 2109 and 2118 support. The first half is a rhetorical question: self-knowledge makes a separate search for the Supreme needless, which continues 2119.

2123.reading: Beyond this eight-span body there is the one with nine gates that takes on beauty; for those who know its coolness and walk by it, eight places come into view, blissful girl.
2123.nuance: The eight-span body and the nine gates are standard; what lies 'beyond' (இதுதாண்டி) the one while being the other is the cipher, perhaps the gross body and the subtle body, or the body and the practice in it. எட்டுத் தலங்கள் may be eight inner stations or the eight siddhis; தண்மை (coolness, or nature) is also open. The next two stanzas repeat இதுதாண்டி for the fort and the pot.

2124.reading: Five persons joined together to rule and built a pleasure-house; know that the Gingee fort you have seen is this, blissful girl.
2124.nuance: The five are the elements (tradition) or the senses; the building is the body, and செஞ்சிக் கோட்டை, the hill fort of Gingee, is a real fort of the poet's country made into its figure. The verse is a riddle of the kind the Siddhars set: the famous fort is the one you are sitting in.

2125.reading: Beyond this filthy carcass, beyond this salted pot, beyond this torn bellows: tend well and become clear, blissful girl.
2125.nuance: Three of Pattinathar's names for the body in one stanza, each with இதுதாண்டி, 'beyond this', from 2123: the body is to be seen through, not merely despised. உப்பிட்ட பாண்டம் is the clay pot cured with salt, kept yet brittle; பீத்தத் துருத்தி the torn wind-skin.

2126.reading: The mother bore me and the father raised me; without taking them for strangers, hear the particulars of this, blissful girl.
2126.nuance: வேத்தாள் is read as வேற்றாள், a stranger. The stanza is a hinge: the plain parents of a plain birth lead into the inquiry of 2127 to 2133, which ends by asking whether those same parents are lasting. A coded reading, with Shakti and Siva as the parents as in 2122, is also possible.

2127.reading: Thinking this carcass great, I sat and wasted my time; when I looked to see which carcass is my own, I did not find one clearly, blissful girl.
2127.nuance: சொந்தச் சடலம், a body that is one's own, is what the search fails to find; the body is held but not owned.

2128.reading: With the woman who delighted in the wedding show, then bearing and raising children, not knowing that it becomes a corpse show, why babble in vain, blissful girl?
2128.nuance: மணக்கோலம் and பிணக்கோலம், wedding array and corpse array, differ by one syllable, and the stanza turns on that rhyme.

2129.reading: When I looked closely into where all things came from, it appeared clearly to me that their origin is in good earth, blissful girl.
2129.nuance: The earth argument of 2129 to 2132: things come from earth, the body's earth is fired into a pot, all things are earth, and what is of earth perishes. மண் is both the element and the soil.

2130.reading: After death they take the body and entomb it, and some days later take that earth and fire it into a pot that serves the people of the world, blissful girl.
2130.nuance: சமாதி here is the burial, as of a siddha, not the yogic state. The body's earth becomes a useful pot: the stanza is matter-of-fact where Tirumular's potter verses are elegiac.

2131.reading: When one pauses to consider that all things are earth, the Lord is there in each of them, clinging like the oil in sesame, blissful girl.
2131.nuance: The sesame image is the Siddhars' standard figure for pervasion that cannot be seen; here it answers the earth argument, so that the reduction of all things to earth does not leave them godless.

2132.reading: What is born on earth perishes; what is watched and kept perishes; what the eye sees perishes: see and know this, blissful girl.

2133.reading: Are the parents who bore you lasting? Are the body, birth and kin lasting? Are the others lasting? Is the wife you took lasting, blissful girl?
2133.nuance: சதம் (lasting, real) is asked five times and never affirmed; Pattinathar's 249 denies the same word seven times and then affirms it of the Lord's feet. The question runs over the chapter break into 2134.

links.note: Both place seed syllables in the body: Agasthiyar sets ஆம், ஓம், வாம், பாம் at the suzhumunai, the moon, the brow and the bow, and Sangili makes Om the body, its mute letter the life, and ரீம், ஸ்ரீம் the way. In both the body is made of mantra, and both leave the key to tradition.

Tirumular counts letters, one, two, three and the great letter, to say how the world, the pair, the light and delusion arise; Sangili makes the letters of Om into body and life. Both verses give only the counts or the letters and leave the decoding to tradition.

Both ride the vaasi: Sivavakkiyar would ride it instead of wearing out his feet on the earth, Sangili's mind mounts the horse called தேசி once the breath is known. In both the horse is the breath and the ride replaces another kind of travel.

Both place the breath's work at the navel: Tirumular raises the prana that stands with the navel whorl to the summit and becomes Siva; Sangili sets the Brahmin's seat in the navel lotus and makes the breath-quest something the knowers never give up.

Both deny that performing worship reaches the Lord by itself: Tirumular's reciters and flower-gatherers have minds like a stone in a moss pond; Sangili says whatever puja one does, the stilling of thought comes by Sadasiva's feet. Tirumular names love as the missing thing, Sangili the stilled mind.

Both turn the great saying into the first person: Tirumular's 'you are that' ripens into 'I have become that' by Nandi's grace; Sangili knows the Siva-Supreme that fills all as 'I myself am I'. Sangili's 2118 has just made the feet the means, so in both the identity is granted, not asserted.

Sivavakkiyar knows all he sees as 'I am he' and still asks when he will take refuge; Sangili knows the Supreme as 'I myself am I' and calls that the supreme quest. Both hold the identity and the search together.

Both run the four paths as a ladder that ends in jnana: Tirumular's devotee goes from kiriyai and chariyai through yoga to the jnana by which the mind becomes Siva; Sangili says that past chariyai, kiriyai and achieved yoga, nothing is of use without jnana. Tirumular credits each rung to grace; Sangili grants grace to the yogi and still says it is not enough.

Sivavakkiyar gives the four paths their four fruits and makes jnana, in all four, reach union; Sangili says the three lower paths and even grace yield nothing without jnana. Both put jnana above the others; Sivavakkiyar grants the others their fruits, Sangili grants them none.

Both count the nine gates and look past them: Sivavakkiyar's nine gates of trouble are left for the good gate and the gate of knowledge, through which one is not born again; Sangili's nine-gated one takes on beauty and shows eight places to those who walk by it. In both the ordinary body's openings are the starting point of a cipher of inner gates.

The Naladiyar's body is a pot that seeps filth from nine openings, and the fool who praises it is deceived by its skin; Sangili's nine-gated one 'takes on beauty' for those who know it. The same nine openings, loathed in the one text, are in the other the thing to be known; Sangili's 2125 then uses the Naladiyar's disgust too.

Both call the body a salted pot (உப்பிட்ட பாண்டம்): Sivavakkiyar asks to become the Lord's subject before it breaks and takes a womb again; Sangili lists it among the things to see beyond. The pot is cured yet brittle in both.

Pattinathar's catalogue, the filthy body, the torn bellows stuffed with flesh and the pot filled with wind, is the source of Sangili's three names; Pattinathar confesses to having loved and carried it, Sangili tells the listener to see past it.
The Kural asks whether the life lodging in the body has no home of its own; Sangili looks for a body that is his own and finds none. Both make the body a place one stays in without owning.

The Naladiyar's wedding drums sound the same day as funeral drums for the bridegroom; Sangili's wedding show (மணக்கோலம்) becomes the corpse show (பிணக்கோலம்). Both rest on a single word changing while the scene stays.

Tirumular's unfired vessel returns to clay when the rain falls, as people die past counting; Sangili sees that all things have their origin in earth and (2132) that what is born of earth perishes. Both argue impermanence from clay.

Tirumular says a broken pot's shards are kept but the broken body is not kept a moment; Sangili says the entombed body's earth is dug up, fired into a pot and serves the world. Sangili does not contradict the abandonment of the corpse, but gives the body's earth a use that Tirumular's verse denies it.

Both use oil in sesame for pervasion: Sivavakkiyar for the end of the Veda that embraces all that moves and stands, Sangili for the Lord clinging in every thing that is earth. In both the pervading thing is present everywhere and visible nowhere.

Tirumular's Lord stands mingled everywhere like jaggery in sugarcane, ghee in milk and scent in the flower; Sangili's Lord clings in all things like oil in sesame. Sangili adds the step that all things are first reduced to earth, so the pervasion holds even of dust.

The Kural calls the lowest understanding the one that takes the impermanent for permanent; Sangili lists what perishes, what is born, what is kept, what is seen, and tells the listener to know it. The Kural judges the error, Sangili supplies the inventory.

Both ask whether parents, body, kin, wife and the rest are சதம், lasting: Pattinathar denies it seven times and affirms it only of the Lord's feet; Sangili asks it five times and answers in 2134 that no one is. Sangili's list is Pattinathar's shortened.

source_issues: 2113 line 4: தானறிந்துய்வாயா runs தான் அறிந்து உய்வாய் together with an extra final ஆ; read as உய்வாய்.
2124 line 4 and 2122 line 2: தெரிந்துக் கொள்வாய் and அறிந் துக்கொண்டு carry a spurious doubled க் after the participle; read தெரிந்து கொள்வாய், அறிந்து கொண்டு.
2126 line 3: வேத்தாள் is not a standard form; read as வேற்றாள் (a stranger). The reading is uncertain.
2128 line 1: பெண் னோடுபின் is split across a space; read பெண்ணோடு பின்.
The chapter division at 2133/2134 cuts the rhetorical question of 2133 from its answer in 2134; the two chapters are one kummi of 36 stanzas.
